implementation_notes: Swift's Golden Hammer is SwiftUI: adopted because it is the modern framework, and then applied to screens whose real requirements are precise control over a video pipeline, a canvas, or a rendering loop the declarative model does not express. The reverse failure is real too — a team that needs custom animation or a Metal-backed view keeps UIKit while management insists every screen be SwiftUI. The measurement is concrete: frame budget, interaction latency, and how much bridging code the framework requires for the specific screen.
idiom_name: SwiftUI applied to every UI, or UIKit where SwiftUI is unavailable
pitfalls: Wrapping a UIKit view in `UIViewRepresentable` for most of the app — the bridging cost is the evidence the requirement did not match the tool.
SwiftData/Core Data chosen before the data shape or migration requirements were known.
Adopting a declarative UI framework for a settings screen because it is the house style rather than because of any requirement.
